Where it began

Ian Botham was born in Heswall, Cheshire, on 24 November 1955, and grew up in Yeovil after his family moved there when he was small. Both his parents played the game: his father for the Westland works club, his mother as captain of a nurses' side. Before he had even started school he would slip through a fence to watch the boys at the local grammar school play, and by nine he was hanging around the town's grounds with his kit, hoping a team would be one short.

He was good enough at football for Crystal Palace to offer him a place, but he decided he was the better cricketer. At sixteen he joined the ground staff at Lord's, selling scorecards and pushing the roller, and at seventeen he made his senior debut for Somerset.

The player

He arrived in Test cricket in July 1977 against Australia at Trent Bridge and took five wickets on the first day. Within a year he had made hundreds and taken eight for 34 against Pakistan at Lord's. In the Jubilee Test in Bombay in 1980 he became the first man to score a hundred and take ten wickets in the same Test.

Across 102 Tests from 1977 to 1992 he made 5,200 runs at 33.55 with 14 hundreds and a best of 208, took 383 wickets at 28.40 with 27 five-wicket hauls, and held 111 catches. For a couple of years in the late 1980s nobody in the world had taken more Test wickets.

What made him special

Botham could change a game in an hour with bat or ball. He bowled lively swing, hit the ball hard but with a straight, proper bat, and was a fine catcher at slip. The summer of 1981 showed all of it. Back in the ranks after giving up the captaincy, he made a hundred at Headingley with England following on and all but beaten, and the Ashes were won from there.

Captaincy was the one job that did not suit him. Most of his twelve Tests in charge came against a great West Indies side, and the runs and wickets dried up for a while. Freed of it, he was himself again within weeks.

Away from the middle

He has spent years raising money for research into childhood leukaemia, more than 13 million pounds of it for Bloodwise, which made him its president. He was knighted, joined the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame in 2009 and was made a life peer, sitting in the House of Lords as a crossbencher. He became chairman of Durham in 2017 and was a familiar voice in the commentary box.

On top of all that, he made eleven Football League appearances for Scunthorpe United, a club he later served as president, and he is a keen golfer and angler.

And finally

When he told his careers teacher he wanted to be a sportsman, the teacher wondered what he was really going to do. A hundred Tests, a knighthood and a seat in the Lords seem a fair answer.
